entry.evidence: the BCF represents a gap in our knowledge of most recent Pleistocene and Holocene slip history

sequences.source_document: Guns et al. 2022, GRL, published PDF

steps.action: Takes from Langenheim and Powell (2009) the cumulative BCF offsets and fault age that give a Ma-scale long-term slip rate of at most 1–2 mm/yr.
steps.quote: provides a Ma-scale long-term slip rate of at most 1–2 mm/yr

steps.action: Poses the question raised by the 1992 Landers and Joshua Tree events: is the BCF being replaced by a newly forming fault system, and what is its most recent slip record?
steps.quote: This unexpected activity sparked a debate about whether or not the PMF or BCF are in fact being replaced by a newly-forming fault system

steps.action: States two rivals with their predictions: under bypass, recent rates fall below the long-term average; at or above the average, the newer fault is not evolving quickly or evolves jointly with the BCF.
steps.quote: its most recent slip rates would likely fall below the long-term fault average

steps.action: Maps two sites 500 m apart on the Hexie Mountains section using 1 m LiDAR and fieldwork, and characterizes seven alluvial surfaces by relative-age attributes and topography.
steps.quote: We use 1 m resolution LiDAR data to identify and map two sites, located 500 m apart

steps.action: Reconstructs six correlated offset surfaces to obtain minimum offsets (channels) and maximum offsets (deposit edges), with preferred offsets where constrained.
steps.quote: We reconstruct correlated surfaces to determine minimum and maximum estimates of fault offset

steps.action: Notes that younger surfaces were deposited atop or reworked older ones after deposition of Qf2b, a possible sign of slip-rate deceleration.
steps.quote: These appear to occur after the deposition of surface Qf2b, perhaps indicating a possible deceleration in slip rate around this time.

steps.action: Collects 38 10Be samples of several types (boulder tops, cobbles, amalgamated pebbles) from each surface to mitigate inheritance and exhumation.
steps.quote: we collected multiple sample types from each surface, including boulder-tops, cobbles, and amalgamated pebble samples

steps.action: Computes 10Be model ages with the exposure age calculator v3 and surface ages with both IsoPlot and the Zechar and Frankel MATLAB tools, and plots kernel density estimates.
steps.quote: We calculate final 10Be model ages using Version 3 of the exposure age calculator described in Balco et al. (2008)

steps.action: Checks the dating premise by comparing ages across sample types that are affected differently by inheritance and exhumation, and finds good agreement (Table S3).
steps.quote: Age agreement between sample types indicates that effects of these processes are negligible

steps.action: Applies Dickinson's (1996) block-rotation equations with Langenheim and Powell's 27–39° rotation to estimate 30–54 km of transferred right-lateral shear, or 4.3–7.7 mm/yr over 7 Ma.
steps.quote: this package of rotating blocks could transfer 4.3–7.7 mm/yr of shear from the SAF in the northern Coachella Valley to the ECSZ

steps.action: Runs Monte Carlo slip-rate regression (Styron Slip Rate Calculator, n = 10,000; boxcar offsets, Gaussian ages) and obtains a best-fit piecewise rate of 2.93 mm/yr before about 71 ka and 0.66 mm/yr after.
steps.quote: produces a best fit piecewise slip rate of 2.93 + 6.14/−1.98 (median, 95% CI) mm/yr before 71 ± 15 (1σ) ka

steps.action: Fits a single long-term rate of 1.26 ± 0.50 mm/yr from the same data and notes that it is a minimum rate on the main strand.
steps.quote: When we fit a single long term slip rate, this data produces a rate of 1.26 ± 0.50 (2σ) mm/yr

steps.action: Repeats the rate fits with preferred offsets instead of min/max offsets, giving 1.56 ± 0.16 mm/yr and a rate change at 69 ± 11 ka (Table 1, Figure 3).
steps.quote: [...] .16 (2σ) when using preferred offsets

steps.action: Computes the total offset over the fault lifetime that the older and younger time-variable rates would predict (about 15–21 km and 3–5 km).
steps.quote: Our best-fit older rate of 2.93 mm/yr produces ∼15–21 km total offset, while our best-fit younger rate of 0.66 mm/yr produces ∼3–5 km total offset.

steps.action: Compares these predictions and the 100 ka long-term rate with the 7–10 km Ma-scale cumulative offset; only the long-term rate matches.
steps.quote: This matches our estimated 100 ka-scale rate of 1.26 mm/yr.

steps.action: Compares the estimated ETR strain transfer of 4.3–7.7 mm/yr with the 4.3–8.1 mm/yr cumulative ECSZ slip rates of Oskin et al. (2008).
steps.quote: These values correspond intriguingly well to the 4.3–8.1 mm/yr cumulative slip rates estimated by Oskin et al. (2008)

steps.action: Sets the apparent rate change beside published slip-rate variability on the Wasatch, SAF, Garlock, White Mountains and San Jacinto faults.
steps.quote: the observation that apparent slip rate can vary within the time window of paleoseismic and geomorphic investigation is not unique

steps.action: Compares the BCF record (no surface rupture since about 13 ka) with the SAF–ECSZ activity cycles of Dolan et al. (2007), which argues against BCF participation in those cycles.
steps.quote: that would indicate that no surface rupturing events have occurred along the BCF since then, while several cycles of activity have occurred

steps.action: Estimates from the 2 m minimum Qf3b offset and Wells and Coppersmith (1994) scaling the earthquakes required: one Mw 7.2 event to five Mw 6.0 events.
steps.quote: would require the occurrence of one ∼MW7.2 to five ∼MW6.0 events

steps.action: Keeps open the rival that the BCF and block rotation are halting as the Eureka Peak Fault takes over, and states that more investigation is needed to evaluate it.
steps.quote: The result that the BCF has recorded a slower slip rate in the recent past can also support an alternative conclusion

steps.action: Keeps a steady long-term slip rate of 1.26 ± 0.50 mm/yr and attributes the apparent variability to natural fluctuation in earthquake strain release.
steps.quote: We argue that the apparent slip rate variability we observe at this site is most likely due to natural fluctuations in strain released by earthquakes

end.claim: The BCF has a long-term late Pleistocene slip rate of 1.26 ± 0.50 (2σ) mm/yr, consistent with its Ma-scale rate, and its apparent rate decrease about 71 ka most likely reflects routine fluctuation about a steady rate.

decisive_move.sentence: The Monte Carlo slip-rate regression combining reconstructed offsets with 10Be surface ages produced both the long-term rate and the piecewise fit on which the steady-rate argument rests.

gates.evidence: The bypass debate and its prediction framed the target, the most recent slip record (p. 2). Mapping and dating, however, follow standard slip-rate practice and are not designed around the rival. The long-term rate could have failed to match the independent Ma-scale 1–2 mm/yr rate (p. 7). The best-fit piecewise rate decrease, which favours the bypass rival, was reinterpreted rather than allowed to count against the steady claim. Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Monte Carlo sampling with linear regression for slip rates; kernel density estimates
Accelerator mass spectrometry for 10Be (LLNL Center for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry)

novelty_claims.quote: New geologic slip rate points to a best fit variable slip rate, with a long-term average slip rate that agrees with regional kinematics
the BCF represents a gap in our knowledge of most recent Pleistocene and Holocene slip history (Figure 1), and we set out here to remedy [...]
in order to calculate an updated range of estimated right lateral shear

limits: Sub-claims and their status: the slip rate of 1.26 ± 0.50 mm/yr is estimate_with_resolution, and it is a minimum because zero erosion is assumed and off-fault deformation is not quantified (p. 6). The 4.3–7.7 mm/yr strain transfer is an estimate that assumes constant block rotation over 7 Ma and uses only published inputs (p. 6). The conclusions give 4.4–7.3 mm/yr instead, an internal inconsistency (p. 8). The piecewise rate decrease at about 71 ka is the statistical best fit (Key Points; p. 6) but is argued away rather than excluded. No formal model-selection test between the single-rate and piecewise fits is reported (inference). The halting/bypass rival is not excluded: its status is no_conclusion (p. 7). The magnitude estimates (Mw 6.0–7.2) are speculative scalings (p. 7). Qf1a is dropped from the rate calculation for lack of a well-constrained age (Table 1). No peer-review file was supplied, although the acknowledgments thank two reviewers for improving the presentation, so no review sequence is coded. Step order follows the text and may not reflect the order of the work (inference). The supporting information was not supplied, so S-figure and S-table checks are coded only from main-text statements.

disagreements.target: Dickinson (1996) assumed fault-lifetime clockwise rotation of ~44°
disagreements.support: The paper replaces the assumed 44° rotation with the 27–39° range of Langenheim and Powell (2009) to update the transferred shear to 30–54 km.
disagreements.quote: Where he assumes a fault-lifetime clockwise block rotation of ∼44° in both cases, we apply a range of 27–39° of clockwise rotation

disagreements.target: Nur et al. (1993) and Hislop (2019): ETR faults being replaced by a newly forming Eureka Peak / Landers-Mojave Earthquake [...]
disagreements.support: The paper argues that the long-term rate, the Ma-scale offsets and the ECSZ strain-transfer match favour a steady BCF, while admitting that the recent slowdown fits the replacement hypothesis.
disagreements.quote: while this hypothesis is certainly possible, more investigation (and time) is required evaluate it

disagreements.target: Dolan et al. (2007) hypothesis of alternating activity cycles between the SAF and ECSZ
disagreements.support: No BCF surface rupture since about 13 ka, while several SAF–ECSZ cycles occurred, suggests the BCF does not record those cycles.
disagreements.quote: no surface rupturing events have occurred along the BCF since then, while several cycles of activity have occurred between the ECSZ [...]
